title: Four Exercises for When You Can't Stop Picking Yourself Apart
hook: Psychologist Diana Hill's approach to appearance obsession doesn't argue with the thought — it changes your relationship to it, so it stops running the day.
key_points: Notice the thought as a thought rather than a fact — 'I'm having the thought that…' creates distance.
Ground yourself in the body's function, not its appearance: what it lets you do today.
Interrupt mirror-checking and comparison loops, which reinforce the fixation each time.
Redirect attention toward what you actually value, so appearance stops crowding it out.
The goal is less energy spent on the thought, not permanently silencing it.
Persistent, distressing appearance preoccupation is worth raising with a clinician.
content_html: Most advice about body image tries to talk you out of the thought. Psychologist Diana Hill, speaking to NPR, takes a different route: the thought is going to show up anyway, so the useful work is changing what it costs you. The first move is simply to label it — "I'm having the thought that I look bad" — which puts a small but real gap between you and a sentence your brain produced.
extra_html:
From there, the exercises shift attention rather than fight it. Ground yourself in what your body does — carried you here, held a plate, slept — instead of how it looks in a photo. Interrupt the checking behaviors, the mirror pass and the scroll-and-compare, because each one buys a moment of relief that makes the next urge stronger. And deliberately redirect toward something you actually care about, since appearance obsession works mostly by crowding everything else out.

None of this promises the thoughts stop, and Hill's framing doesn't pretend otherwise. The goal is that they take up less of your energy. If the preoccupation is persistent and genuinely distressing, that's a reason to talk to a clinician rather than push harder on your own.

flashcards.prompt: What is the aim of these body-image exercises?

choices.text: To change your relationship to the thought so it takes less energy
To argue the thought down until it's proven false
To eliminate all thoughts about appearance permanently

flashcards.explanation_html: The approach doesn't debate the content of the thought. Noticing it as a thought, grounding in what your body does, and redirecting to your values loosen its grip.

flashcards.prompt: Why does mirror-checking make appearance fixation worse?
flashcards.back_html: Each check briefly relieves the anxiety, which reinforces the loop and makes the next urge stronger. Interrupting the checking is part of breaking the cycle.

flashcards.prompt: When does appearance preoccupation warrant professional help?
flashcards.back_html: When it's persistent and genuinely distressing, or it's eating into daily life. That's a clinician conversation, not a willpower problem.
